subject: chemistry
title: Uncertainty in measurements
key_idea: Every measurement has some uncertainty. Repeat the readings, leave out anomalous results and find the mean. The range of the readings about the mean is a measure of uncertainty, written as mean ± uncertainty.

blocks.text: Every measurement has some uncertainty. Taking repeat readings and finding the mean gives a more reliable value.

items.meaning: The range of the readings about the mean: the greatest amount any reading is above or below the mean. It is shown as a ± value.
The largest reading minus the smallest reading. It can be written as from the smallest reading to the largest.
A result that does not fit the pattern. It is left out of the mean.

blocks.label: Mean
blocks.formula: mean = total of the readings ÷ number of readings
where: readings in the same unit, such as °C or g

items: Leave out any anomalous result before calculating the mean.
Example: 0.84 g, 0.79 g, 0.86 g and 0.47 g. The 0.47 g is anomalous.
Repeat readings, then find the mean.
Do not include an anomalous result in the mean.

blocks.text: The range of the repeat readings about the mean is used as a measure of uncertainty. The uncertainty is shown after the mean as ± a value.

items: Find the mean of the readings.
Find how far each reading is above or below the mean.
The largest of these differences is the uncertainty.
If the readings are spread evenly either side of the mean, this is half the range.

blocks.label: Uncertainty
blocks.formula: uncertainty = largest difference between a reading and the mean
where: readings and mean in the same unit

items: Highest temperature reached in four trials: 37.6 °C, 37.2 °C, 37.8 °C and 37.4 °C.
Differences from the mean: 0.1, 0.3, 0.3 and 0.1 °C. The largest is 0.3 °C.
Result: 37.5 ± 0.3 °C. The readings lie between 37.2 °C and 37.8 °C.
Another set: 6, 9, 10 and 11 cm³ has a mean of 9 cm³. The differences are 3, 0, 1 and 2, so the result is 9 ± 3 cm³.

diagram.alt: Calculate the uncertainty from four repeat readings.
diagram.question: Four repeat readings of the highest temperature were {a} °C, {b} °C, {c} °C and {d} °C. Calculate the uncertainty: the largest difference between a reading and the mean. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

answer.formula: max(max(max(a, b), max(c, d)) - (a + b + c + d) / 4, (a + b + c + d) / 4 - min(min(a, b), min(c, d)))

working: Uncertainty = largest difference between a reading and the mean = {answer} °C

items: The uncertainty is the range about the mean.
Uncertainty = the largest difference between a reading and the mean.
Write the result as mean ± uncertainty, with the unit.

blocks.text: Questions ask you to calculate mean ± uncertainty, or to explain what the ± value shows.

diagram.alt: Put the steps for finding mean plus or minus uncertainty in order.
steps: Add the remaining readings and divide by how many there are to find the mean
Find how far each reading is from the mean
Take the largest difference as the uncertainty
Write the result as mean ± uncertainty, with the unit

items: The ± value is the uncertainty.
It is the range about the mean value.
The readings are a maximum of that value either side of the mean.
Example: 16.5 ± 0.3 °C means readings from 16.2 °C to 16.8 °C.
State that the ± value is the uncertainty.
Explain that it is the range about the mean, with readings that much either side.

checks.q: Four readings are 37.6, 37.2, 37.8 and 37.4 °C. Calculate the mean and give the uncertainty.
checks.a: Mean = 150 ÷ 4 = 37.5 °C. The largest difference from the mean is 37.8 − 37.5 = 0.3 °C. Result: 37.5 ± 0.3 °C.

checks.q: A mean temperature is recorded as 16.5 ± 0.3 °C. Explain what ± 0.3 °C shows.
checks.a: It is the uncertainty. It is the range about the mean value, so readings are a maximum of 0.3 °C either side of the mean.

checks.q: Results are 0.84 g, 0.79 g, 0.86 g and 0.47 g, and 0.47 g is anomalous. Calculate the mean.

worked_example.question:
A student repeated an experiment four times using 0.50 g of zinc powder.

The table shows the results.

| | Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3 | Trial 4 |
| Highest temperature reached in °C | 37.6 | 37.2 | 37.8 | 37.4 |

Calculate the mean highest temperature reached.

Include the uncertainty in your answer.

Mean highest temperature reached = _____ ± _____ °C
worked_example.tip: One mark for the method, one for the mean and one for the uncertainty.
